faq_items.question: What are good preschool activities to do at home?
faq_items.answer: Good at-home options are open-ended and hands-on: sorting buttons or socks by color, scoop-and-pour bins with beans or water, playdough, sticker and dot-marker pages, indoor obstacle courses, and pretend play. Rotate a few each morning to cover fine motor, language, and gross-motor skills without any special supplies.

faq_items.question: How many hours a day should you do preschool activities at home?
faq_items.answer: Aim for just 20 to 30 minutes of structured, adult-led activity at a time, in two or three short blocks across the day. The rest should be free play, outdoor time, and rest. Preschoolers focus for only a few minutes per year of age, so short and frequent beats one long lesson.

faq_items.question: How do I do preschool at home for free?
faq_items.answer: Use household items as materials: pasta and beans for sorting, cardboard boxes for building, painter's tape for hopscotch and roads, and a muffin tin for color sorting. Keep basics like markers, glue, and paper on hand, then plan one focus skill per day. A free printable planner keeps it organized at zero cost.

faq_items.question: What should a 4-year-old be learning at home?
faq_items.answer: Focus on five areas: fine motor (cutting, threading), gross motor (balance, coordination), language and literacy (read-alouds, rhyming), early math (counting, patterns, sorting), and social-emotional skills (sharing, naming feelings, taking turns). Touch each one across the week through play rather than drilling worksheets, and skills develop naturally.

faq_items.question: How do I keep my preschooler busy without screens?
faq_items.answer: Set activities up on a tray or in a bin so they have clear edges, rotate toys so a few feel new each week, and prep two or three options the night before. Ready-to-grab stations — sorting, playdough, obstacle courses, pretend play — keep a preschooler engaged far longer than an open toy shelf and no plan.
